description.narrative: 1.DNDi goal is to finalize the development of an all-new, single-dose oral drug, acoziborole, that can be given at the point of care in primary healthcare settings. If successful, the treatment would provide a powerful boost to efforts to achieve the WHO target of sustainably eliminating sleeping sickness as a public health problem. 2. Until acoziborole is registered, DNDi continues to promote access to fexinidazole for both forms of sleeping sickness by supporting national control programmes and strengthening pharmacovigilance systems in endemic countries.3. DNDi is prioritizing young children needs through a collaboration with African and European experts in the ACOZI-KIDS consortium on a clinical trial of single-dose acoziborole to make treatment for children with sleeping sickness much simpler – and less painful.

DNDi and partners have revolutionized the treatment of sleeping sickness since its founding in 2003. In 2009, working closely with Epicentre, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute, and the national HAT control programmes of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Republic of the Congo, DNDi completed the development of nifurtimox and eflornithine combined treatment (NECT), a safer treatment for the advanced stage of the most common form of the disease, caused by T.b. gambiense. In 2018, DNDi, Sanofi, and partners delivered fexinidazole, a paradigm-changing all-oral treatment for both stages of T.b. gambiense sleeping sickness. In a further success for DNDi and partners, the treatment’s indication is now being expanded to include the less common but more acute form of the disease caused by T.b. rhodesiense. Fexinidazole is donated to the World Health Organization (WHO) by Sanofi’s Foundation S for distribution to all national sleeping sickness control programmes.

title.narrative: 2009: NECT: better, safer treatment for sleeping sickness

description.narrative: Before 2009, the best treatment for sleeping sickness, eflornithine, was very complex to distribute and administer in regions affected by the disease. All too often, doctors would have no choice but to use melarsoprol, a highly toxic, arsenic-based drug that killed one of every 20 patients it was meant to cure.In 2009, results from a pivotal clinical trial sponsored by DNDi and Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) showed that Nifurtimox-eflornithine combination therapy (NECT), a combined treatment of Bayer’s nifurtimox and Sanofi’s eflornithine, was a safe and effective treatment for sleeping sickness. NECT has significant practical benefits in comparison to eflornithine: there are fewer intravenous infusions (14 instead of 56), treatment length is shorter, and it is more cost effective than using eflornithine alone. NECT is not only better for patients, but it also simplifies the logistics and staffing needed at treatment centres, which are often in remote areas.

title.narrative: Number of patients treated with NECT in HAT endemic regions

description.narrative: Since 2017, more than 646 patients have been treated with NECT in Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Congo, Guinea, Cameroon, Gabon and Tchad.

title.narrative: 2021: Fexinidazole: First new chemical entity developed by DNDi and the first all-oral cure for T.b. gambiense sleeping sickness

description.narrative: Fexinidazole is the first all-oral treatment for both stages of T.b. gambiense sleeping sickness, the most common form of the disease. Fexinidazole is an oral pill taken for 10 days, offering practical advantages over the previous standard of care, NECT, because it eliminates the need for systematic hospitalization and leads to a reduction in the number of lumbar punctures. The European Medicines Agency adopted a positive scientific opinion on fexinidazole in late 2018, paving the way for registration and distribution in endemic countries. The drug was registered in the Democratic Republic of Congo in December 2018 and in Uganda in October 2021. Other endemic countries are using fexinidazole through special authorisations of their ministries of health.

title.narrative: Number of patients treated with fexinidazole in HAT endemic regions

description.narrative: Fexinidazole is distributed since 2019 in Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). More than 289 patients have beneficiated from a World Health Organization distribution programme between 2019 and 2021 in DRC, Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea, Guinea, Gabon and Tchad.
